clue.text: 9 6 16 church has half of Room 101 at the front

indicators.note: the numeral is placed at the front, before the church
this word only joins the neighbouring pieces: it says which one stands next to which in the answer

parts.note: in Roman numerals 101 is C (100) plus I (1)
CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word means its first two letters

explanation.surface: A church has the room-number sign from Orwell's torture chamber mounted at its entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Room 101' looks like one unit, Orwell's chamber, but it splits into half of 'Room' and the Roman numeral for 101.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman orator and statesman is a classic long-dead male writer of the European canon.

clue.text: Going from either end over diocese, travelling the shortest route

indicators.note: in a down entry, this letter goes above the rest
the word Going starts and ends with the same letter, so taking it from either end gives the same letter
travelling suggests the letters are moving about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bishop's journey across the diocese, taking the most direct path.
explanation.walkthrough: G is the letter at both ends of 'Going'; 'travelling' rearranges DIOCESE to EODESIC.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry this word names the shortest line between two points on a curved surface.

clue.text: 9 6 16 dunking roll in tea? The opposite

indicators.note: dunking says one thing is plunged into another
with dunking, says one piece goes inside the other
the opposite tells us to reverse the roles, putting the tea inside the roll rather than the roll inside the tea

parts.note: a bun is a bread roll
cha is slang for tea

explanation.surface: A writer seen dunking a bread roll into a cup of tea, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as roll inside tea; 'The opposite' swaps which piece holds the other, so the tea ends up within the roll.
explanation.definitionFit: John Buchan, Scottish author of The Thirty-Nine Steps, is a long-dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Discrimination, the charge against 9 6 16s?

definitions.meaning: a preference for a select few, treating them as superior
critics accuse the traditional canon of favouring a privileged few

explanation.surface: Critics accuse the old canon of discrimination.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a belief in rule by a superior few, which is both a form of discrimination and the usual complaint about the canon.

clue.text: Barman's wife is in bed

definitions.note: the 's stands for is: a barman is a man of the Bar, the legal profession

indicators.note: the wife's letter is placed inside the bed

parts.note: a layer is a bed, as of rock or soil

explanation.surface: A pub barman's wife has gone to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' suggests a pub; here it is a member of the Bar, the body of barristers.
explanation.definitionFit: Barristers practise at the Bar, so a barman in this sense is a legal professional.

clue.text: See 9
In unpleasant way, skin horribly lousy

parts.note: hide is an animal's skin

indicators.note: horribly suggests the letters are mangled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's skin is described as horribly lousy, unpleasantly infested.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in a revolting or ugly manner, a stronger form of unpleasantly.

clue.text: 9 6 16, eccentric American

parts.note: in engineering a cam is an eccentric, an off-centre wheel
US means American, as in United States

explanation.surface: A writer described as an eccentric American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like an anagram signal or an adjective; it is a noun, the engineering term for a cam.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus, the French author of The Outsider, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: We dominate, are pale-hued; ripe for revision, me?

definitions.note: the speaker of the clue, the figure whose letters are being reshuffled, is the thing defined

indicators.note: something ripe for revision is due to be reworked, so the preceding words are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A self-portrait: a privileged pale-skinned group admits its dominance and that it is overdue for a rethink.
explanation.walkthrough: The twenty-one letters of 'We dominate, are pale-hued' are rearranged; the clue is spoken by the subject itself, hence 'me?'. This phrase is the puzzle's theme: many clues use '9 6 16' for a writer who fits it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a critical label for the canon of long-gone Western writers, which the speaker of the clue claims to be.

clue.text: 9 6 16 attributed to Reagan?

parts.note: a work attributed to someone is by them
Ron is the short form of Ronald, as in Ronald Reagan

explanation.surface: A quotation by a famous writer misattributed to President Reagan.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron, the Romantic poet, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: 9 6 16 is up to receive top honours

indicators.note: the reversed word takes the honours inside it
in a down entry, up means the word is is written from bottom to top

parts.note: in card games the ace and king, A and K, are the top honours

explanation.surface: A writer is set to receive the highest honours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is up' reverses IS to SI, which then receives AK.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, the Edwardian short-story writer, a dead white European male.

clue.text: 9 6 16 Jack, leading scorer in two legs

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in cards

indicators.note: the scorer's letter goes between the two copies
two says the word for leg appears twice

parts.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side, so on means leg

indicators.note: leading means the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A footballer called Jack is the top scorer over two legs of a tie.
explanation.walkthrough: A tie played home and away has two legs, but here each leg is ON, the cricket on side, with S between.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Jonson, the Jacobean playwright, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Seabird never rejected skin of shark

parts.note: a shag is a kind of cormorant

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ne'er is the poetic contraction of never

explanation.surface: A seabird has never turned down a shark's skin as food.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names rough rawhide or sharkskin used as an abrasive or for covering cases.

clue.text: Our team in African capital find cold reception

parts.note: we stands for our team

indicators.note: the capital finds cold within it

parts.note: Lomé is the capital of Togo
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: A touring side arriving in an African capital get a frosty greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold reception' reads as one phrase; only 'reception' is the definition and 'cold' gives C.
explanation.definitionFit: A greeting given to someone arriving, as in a warm or cold reception.

clue.text: Rising, point to foreign character: "Beware void!"

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the pieces are read from the bottom up

parts.note: E, east, is a compass point
tau is a letter of the Greek alphabet
cave is Latin for beware, as in schoolboy slang

explanation.surface: A Greek letter on a warning sign shouting 'Beware the void!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'void' looks like a noun in the warning; it is the verb, to empty.
explanation.definitionFit: To void a space is to empty it, the same as clearing everyone or everything out.

clue.text: See 9
9 6 16 with Richard, regulars at tennis

parts.note: Dick is a short form of Richard

indicators.note: regulars means the letters taken at regular intervals, every other one

explanation.surface: A writer playing doubles with Richard, both regulars at the tennis club.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens, the Victorian novelist, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: 9 6 16's work: regal ruin, as family's taken over

indicators.note: in a down entry, the family is placed over the rest

parts.note: kin means family

indicators.note: ruin suggests the word is wrecked, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer's work about royal ruin after the family seizes power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruin' rearranges REGAL to GLEAR, with KIN above it; the surface neatly sums up the play's plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy is a work by a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Tick on list, we hear, 9 6 16

indicators.note: we hear says the words are spoken and sound like the entry

parts.note: to tick something on a list is to check it off

explanation.surface: Someone ticking items on a list.
explanation.definitionFit: Anton Chekhov, the Russian playwright and story writer, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Pipe turned in spiral shape almost by old woman

indicators.note: turned means the whole is turned round and read backwards
by means beside, the old woman following
almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a helix is a spiral shape
gran is a familiar word for grandmother

explanation.surface: A pipe turned into a spiral shape, nearly, by an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah, the oriental water pipe in which smoke is drawn through water.

clue.text: 9 6 16 massaged ego, then stopped short

indicators.note: massaged suggests the word is worked over, so its letters are rearranged
stopped short means the last letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A writer had his ego massaged, then was abruptly cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the German author of Faust, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Glower, about to lend out

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are disordered, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone glares, about to lend something out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glower' reads as scowl; it is glow-er, a thing that glows.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax light that glows when lit is, playfully, something that glows.

clue.text: 9 6 16 hoax involving American gunmen

indicators.note: involving means taking the other piece inside

parts.note: cod as an adjective means sham or mock, a hoax
the NRA is the National Rifle Association of America

explanation.surface: A writer caught up in a hoax with American gunmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hoax' is COD, as in a cod accent, not CON.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Conrad, Polish-born British author of Heart of Darkness, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: 9 6 16 part of Germany, more central

parts.note: a Land is a German federal state

indicators.note: central means the middle letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A writer from part of Germany, more centrally placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Savage Landor, the English poet, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: 9 6 16, usually first in a haunt of vice

indicators.note: the first letter is put inside the other words

parts.note: a den is a haunt of vice, as in a den of iniquity

indicators.note: first means the first letter of the word usually

explanation.surface: A writer usually found in a den of iniquity first.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden, the English poet, is a dead white European male writer.

clue.text: Scrooge, say, broke, about to chuck last bit away

indicators.note: about means going round the other piece

parts.note: skint is British slang for broke, penniless

indicators.note: the last letter is taken away

parts.note: to fling is to chuck

explanation.surface: Scrooge, being broke, is about to throw away the last scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Scrooge is the classic miser, an example of a stingy person.

clue.text: Dog refusing lead at end of day, troubled by fleas?

indicators.note: at says the next letter comes alongside
refusing lead means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a bitch is a female dog

indicators.note: end of means the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A dog refuses its lead at the end of the day, bothered by fleas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' is a dog's leash in the picture, but means the first letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: Flea bites leave the skin irritated, wanting to be scratched; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: John's eating no end of sausage in place in New Mexico

indicators.note: eating means taking the other piece inside

parts.note: john is slang for a toilet, and loos are toilets; the 's makes the plural

indicators.note: no end of means the last letter is removed

parts.note: salami is a sausage

explanation.surface: John is eating a sausage, all but the end, somewhere in New Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: The town is where the atomic bomb was developed, a site in that US state.
